utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances, first of all, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. With a very odd LiveNote, it's Joanna Korner, Alexis Demirdjian and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a couple of matters before the witness comes into court. The first is this: As you know, he was ordered to bring up the originals of the diaries and his military booklet. I haven't had an opportunity to see whether the original of his military booklet is there, but the diaries are certainly there and it doesn't appear that he has brought anything extra. However, there's a whole bunch, if I can put it that way, of other documents and at the moment I'm not clear, because we haven't had a chance to look at them, exactly what they are. Additionally, he has brought some CDs which appear to contain videos which are new. Now, Your Honours, I think we can get started. It may be the simplest is to ask him what he has brought with him before we go any further. Whether that's done by myself or Your Honours, I don't know. I think we need to see what it all amounts to. The second matter is this: Mr. Krgovic last, whenever it was, Thursday, I think, told Your Honours that the only extra questions he wanted to ask were limited to entries from the diary, and Your Honours gave him leave. This morning, we've received a total of some further nine documents that Mr. Krgovic apparently wishes to use in cross-examination. Three are the diaries, we have no objection to that. The others are documents that he could have used in his original cross-examination. And, Your Honours, we therefore say, he could have dealt with it then, the leave that he has been given to re-open his cross-examination is limited to the diaries. It's a matter for Your Honours having heard from Mr. Krgovic whether you grant him leave to use the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not want my cross-examination to be limited to the diaries. I wanted it to be limited to the topics that I have touched upon before, and that was the original objection by Ms. Korner. We were talking about topics from my previous cross-examination. The new documents that I mention here are related to the topics, and those documents also explain the entries made by this witness and this will be the purpose of my cross-examination. That was my original statement. My new cross-examination will not go any further, anywhere beyond the topics that I have already examined about. Many of the topics are mentioned in the entries in the diaries and those new documents relate to those topics and those entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Ms. Korner, it appears that the problem that you thought exist doesn't really exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a problem. He could have dealt with the topics which are dealt with in those documents outside the diaries at the time. Your Honours, there has to be a limit on what you can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded by the objections raised by the -- Ms. Korner and the leave granted to Mr. Krgovic would be -- is going to be applied to allow him to deal with the -- these documents that have just become the subject of this dispute. You wanted to say something, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, about the first matter, if I can be of any assistance to the Trial Chamber. First of all, it was my understanding that Ms. Korner insisted that the witness brings the originals of the documents that he provided to the OTP with him, so I assume those are the documents because I haven't seen them. Now, about the four videos, the four videos as far as we could have seen in the couple of minutes that we have before, one video is concerning the crime in Sijekovac which happened on the 27th of March, where, if you remember, the Croatian troops crossed to Bosnia and committed a crime in one Serbian village. The other is some tape of the TV show where this person Anto Prkacin, who was the head of that particular unit, is talking because, I couldn't hear what he was -- but I assume again that this concerns this crime in Sijekovac. The third is some video of a camp in Turlak in Bosanski Brod, which I wasn't aware of the existence of that camp but I assume that is the camp which the Croat forces kept in Bosanski Brod. Therefore, I don't think it's relevant. And the fourth one, I'm sorry, it escaped me right now, I'm not sure. But again I don't think any of these -- any of these videos are immediately relevant for the subject matter of this case, but of course, Your Honours will ask the witness about it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is a matter which the Chamber wishes to raise in private session and after that is resolved, there are certain -- it has been brought to the attention of the Chamber that there are certain concerns that the witness has which we also need to deal with in private session. But before we move into private session, I wonder if there are any other housekeeping matters that we need address? In which case we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And while the witness is on his way in, Mr. Zecevic, it would be -- is a reminder from the Chamber to be grateful from your batting order until the recess, end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It would be no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot guarantee the dates, because -- but the batting order, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course the time needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. Well, there is still one matter which is pending and that is a decision on videolink witnesses. We requested a videolink for two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which ruling should be issued shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could the usher please escort the witness back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, good morning to you, sir. Welcome back to the Tribunal. Because of the lengthy interruption in your testimony, I would invite you to make the solemn declaration again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before Ms. Korner -- before your cross-examination resumes, I think it's Mr. Krgovic who would go first, there are certain matters in respect of which we would have to go into private session which we now do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And there is a question, Mr. Bjelosevic, before counsel continues, which because of the -- your status as a sworn witness, counsel not having any contact with you, I suppose the Chamber is in the best position to ask, and that is for you to let us know what documents you have brought with you since the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've brought with me what had been required to be provided during my testimony, namely, I made photocopies of specific documents. And with the aid of your staff who came to Sarajevo, I dispatched this starting with this booklet, then proceeding with my diaries from the relevant period, bulletins of daily events, reports of certain security issues relating to that period that the service acquired, and today I also brought four CDs that also pertained to the year 1992. All of these are short entries but I think that, nonetheless, each one of them speaks quite clearly about specific things that I addressed in my previous testimony and also probably some things that we are going to speak during the continuation of my testimony. And I also brought a book that was mentioned here written by a group of authors, a group of journalists from 1992, this is the original in German and the translation into Serbian. And I would like to offer this as well. I think this will be very helpful for everyone to take a look at. I did not make any photocopies. You have two versions in two languages, so it's up to you which one you decide to choose. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just ask Your Honours perhaps to ask at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I was going to invite you by way of clarification to, yourself, ask the witness if the general question that the Chamber phrased wasn't adequate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I may then, although this is all a bit odd because Mr. Krgovic is going to re-cross examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, are any of the paper documents that you have brought up today ones which were not photocopied earlier and given to VWS, leaving aside the diaries, please, and the German book? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure when you spoke about my journals that I understood you properly. They have been photocopied but I brought the originals for comparison and also the book, and as I said, it's the book written in German and translated into Serbian. And there is also a number of documents that we mentioned awhile ago, so all of that I brought as photocopies and I also brought the originals for the sake of comparison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, thank you for that. But all I am concerned about is forgetting the journals, forgetting the book, the wads of paper that we can see you brought, were they all photocopied and given to VWS or are there new documents that you did not give to VWS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four CDs have not been copied. I handed them over. That also applies to the book and also to a number of documents that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's what I thought. Are you able yourself to identify which documents that you brought up today you have not previously photocopied and given to VWS? Are they in a separate bundle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think this will delay matters today, but obviously we are going to ask that those documents are handed over to VWS again for photocopies to be made today hopefully in the break for us on the Defence, then we can see what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic. I finished my cross-examination. However, due to the emergence of new documents which I'll have to go back again to discuss your journals and the events that you described in your notes. Only one thing I'd like to clarify first. If I understood you correctly, all the documents that you provided to the VWS you copied, but there is a portion that you still haven't provided to the VWS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these documents relate to 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, one question relating to your journal, we are in receipt of photocopies of the three journals. Are those notes of yours contemporaneous notes, do they describe the events that happened in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that covers a period 1991 and 1992, and it covers the places where the meetings took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you subsequently did not enter any changes? This is authentic document and your authentic notes as you made them at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have the originals here and I believe that the forensics is so advanced nowadays that if anyone wants to make any comparison and make confirmation of the authenticity, it can easily be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, let us go through some of your entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can I please have in e-court Exhibit 2D101169. Your Honours, this is a portion of -- that's tab 5 in Zupljanin Defence. It's tab 017 and it's a Prosecution Exhibit 2103.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If it is easier for you, Mr. Bjelosevic, you can see that this is an entry that you made on the 11th of July, 1992, so maybe you can find your bearings easier in that way.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this first part of your entry in which you speak about, or, rather, you noted down the debate. I see on the left-hand side it says "Zupljanin and Banja Luka." Does that mean that you recorded what Stojan Zupljanin was saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin spoke on behalf of the Banja Luka CSB, and then I can see what other participants said, but I'm particularly interested in this portion where you say under bullet number 2 that Mr. Zupljanin says, "Engage the police for conduct of combat operations"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please turn off the mike while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the engagement of the police in combat operation presented a great problem, because the army quite often would take over the whole police force of a police station and take them to the front line leaving the police station practically devoid of the necessary number of police officers necessary to carry out regular police work?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me elaborate a bit on this. On several occasions, I had some live communication with Mr. Lisica at the time about this subject. I don't want to leave the impression that I am complaining about what Commander Lisica was doing because defence had always been priority number one in our areas. And I fully understand that once he wrote to me after I complained about the lack of police officers for maintaining public law and order, he responded by saying if this goes on and if the front line becomes weak and we have enemy forces capturing Doboj, you will have no one to keep the law and order over. And as a commander, he was completely right in thinking so. He had the right to engage all the forces in the area of his responsibility because defence was the priority number one. However, that produced a negative ramifications on the public law and order, the safety of property of people -- and people. And all chiefs of centres highlighted this as a problem in this meeting as one of the critical problems affecting the functioning of the surface during this chaotic war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly look at Exhibit P160 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have one intervention, Your Honours. I note that the translation of this page of the diary is inadequate. Perhaps the witness can read for the record or we should resend this for revision of the translation because it says, "Question of jurisdiction of military authorities in MUP," which is a wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps we need do both, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Krgovic, could you ask the witness to read from the original. Can we get the translation on the record and then have the exhibit resubmitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will recall this is all being done at top speed with the assistance of Your Honours. I am afraid that is something that's going to happen. And at the moment, it will have to go on the back burner because they are still trying to translate the other entries. So it can't go back and be immediately corrected if it's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, that's the second phase, but for the time being if the witness's oral recitation of the contents could be interpreted, at least that's a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll do this but first I want to finish this subject and then we go back to the journal. I asked the question about the first entry, but then after that, we'll proceed. So can he now be shown P160, tab 66 of Stanisic's Defence, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that, Mr. Bjelosevic, you don't have this binder with you. Therefore, would you be could kind to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's ERN number 0324-1855, tab 66 of the Defence of Stanisic. Page 8 in e-court in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the fourth paragraph from the top?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's your page 5 but in e-court it's page 8. You can see the page number in the top corner.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This portion has been partially translated, so I'm going to read it out to you carefully which reads that: "Because of the casualties in Mrkonjic Grad, 20 active duty and reserve police members were killed in one operation alone. Define the role of the police and its direct engagement in combat activities and, related to this, the reinforcements. The army is asking for the engagement of the full force, want them to be re-subordinated and pushed to the most difficult lines but this should be prevented." Mr. Bjelosevic, this is basically the problem that was discussed in this meeting of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took notes, very briefly, that would serve as a reminder for myself, but here in this contribution of Mr. Zupljanin was recorded in this minutes of the meeting and as I said, all chiefs of the centres pin-pointed this problem about the engagement of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as what Mr. Zupljanin said is concerned, could you please read out this last bullet point, the question of authority. So could you please go back to your diary. Could you please go back to your diary. So that is, again, 2D101169. Could you please read out aloud this last bullet point that says, "The question of authority, the military authorities and the MUP." That is where Mr. Zupljanin asked for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to have a delineation of authority. So it is the question of authority of the military authorities and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, this was a problem that you were facing as well and that is that there wasn't a clear distinction between what who was in charge of. So what was requested was to state exactly what the authority of the MUP was and what the authority of the military was; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that it would be right to take the break now. Perhaps we could adjourn at this point and I'm going to move on to something else afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I expect that counsel have got the same report we have, that the technical problems have been somewhat corrected, but we are still not perfect yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, let us proceed. Could you please look at the next entry in your diary. That is 2D101178, tab 6 of the Zupljanin Defence. For you that is the entry of the 27th of August, 1992. It's the second page in English. Mr. Bjelosevic, from this page onwards over a few pages you record some information that has to do with these persons who were in Teslic. And you also say who sent them there and how that happened; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it necessary for us to move into private session now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are going to be discussing this, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought the reasoning was that there should be an explanation. I think I know what this is, but I think Mr. Krgovic should ask what he is recording there and we'll see that it doesn't require private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I'm a bit nervous about exploring reasons in open session, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can we take a look at another entry, 2D101187. It's tab number 7 of Zupljanin Defence and that's the 9th of September, 1992. Mr. Bjelosevic, this is a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 9th of September, 1992. Is that the meeting that we mentioned the last time that I examined you, the meeting that was attending by Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the first entry, we see a mention of a dispatch seeking release or change of jurisdiction to the high court in Doboj. And then under number 2, they mention the amount of foreign currency found in the safe of the SJB, and then there's the issue of the official identification card, the accommodation of the indicted persons, the release of people from prison. So those are the topics discussed at this meeting. We are now going to take a look at another document, but I think that most of the persons mentioned were at liberty at the time. This was some sort of post factum analysis of what had been done.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As the interpreter translator couldn't read the word "seeking of release of," could he tell us what that word is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the penultimate dash, "release of persons from the prison in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, "9th of September, 1, dispatch seeking release of ...," blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, could you please read carefully the whole paragraph under number 1. Could you please read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dispatch seeking release or handing over into the jurisdiction of the high court in Doboj." And I put a question mark here because a dispatch had been sent by the court in Doboj to the court in Banja Luka seeking that in accordance with the jurisdiction, people who were deprived of the liberty in Teslic should be transferred to the prison in Doboj, and I also want that topic to be discussed. We should have examined who signed this order. There was another dispatch sent on behalf of the Security Services Centre in Doboj, my name was typed but it was signed by Milan Savic. So those are the issues that we discussed. And now that we are talking about this, if you take a look at the third dash from the bottom, accommodation of those persons and their food. I had the principle objection, regardless of the fact that they were suspects, I thought that they should have been issued with an order about their detention the moment they were detained. That's what I wanted explained, the kind of treatment that they received. And that's what we discussed. There is one thing that I did not write in. I wanted the investigation to encompass also the death of two persons, one of them came with the third group from Doboj, and another of them was from Teslic. If I remember his name, it was Tjecanin [phoen]. So as far as I knew at the time, the investigation did not pertain to that and that's why I insisted that the investigation should pertain to it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, there is an intervention concerning the translation. Your Honours will see that the original document has five dashes, the entries. The first is Inspector Markovic, then official identification card, and then the third dash which the witness actually was commenting just now was not translated in the English translation. The English translation has only four dashes and the original has five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful for Mr. Zecevic. I couldn't think what he was talking about because I couldn't see it either. Could he read that again, the dash that's omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, could you please read out aloud all the dashes, or maybe just the third one, just the third dash?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can list them all. However the third one says, "Accommodation of arrested persons." And then the next one is "Release of people from the prison in Banja Luka." Should I read out the rest?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. I'm going to ask you a question. Mr. Bjelosevic, you mentioned two dispatches that you discussed. One of them was signed on your behalf. You mean the dispatch that was shown to you by Mr. Zecevic during the examination-in-chief, the one that was signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the second dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P1314. That's tab 8 in the Zupljanin binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you can see the document now. The president of the higher court in Doboj sent it to the president of the Banja Luka high court saying that bearing in mind the territorial jurisdiction and the subject matter jurisdiction, those persons should be transferred from Banja Luka to the detention in Doboj and that was done.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document that I mentioned and that's it. You know, there were many manipulations and various interpretations of what was going on and who requested what and who did not request other things, and that's why we held that meeting in order to clarify some of those issues. The investigative judge was present, the Prosecutor, Mr. Zupljanin, I was present. I don't remember other people but those that I've just mentioned, they most definitely did attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when they were transferred, those persons were then handed over to the jurisdiction of the court and judicial organs in Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their fate in relation to the judicial process, so to speak. I don't know which organ was in charge of that. However, they were transferred from the Banja Luka prison to the Doboj prison. Now, I cannot claim that with any certainty, but I think that the same day or the day after, some of them were sent to attend -- to be attended by doctors, but anyway, they were released. I suppose that the whole proceedings continued in the Teslic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 2D88. It's tab number 3 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. 2D88.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, this is ruling by the Teslic lower court which cancel the detention for some persons on the 21st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph you can see that the public prosecutor in Teslic agreed to this release; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, so you know that all those persons were transferred to the Doboj prison where they spent some time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. I think they were even transferred there by a prison bus belonging to the Doboj prison, but whether they were released on the same day or on the following day, I do not know. However, later on they were all released and now I see the decision on termination of their detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you Exhibit P1313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I may not have understood the point you wished to make here, but could I ask you of the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have heard testimony before this Chamber -- or, part of the Prosecution case is that those persons were released with the agreement of Stojan Zupljanin. We even heard testimony that some of them were released without even being detained in the Doboj prison, a witness testified to that effect in closed session. I want to show through these documents that this is incorrect and that they were released in accordance with the documents that I have just shown to the witness. Therefore, Stojan Zupljanin had nothing to do with these proceedings once the criminal report had been filed, that's what I want to show here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P1313, page 30 in English and in Serbian. And I'm going to give you a photocopy so that you can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, take a look at 144.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see Miroslav Pijunovic, Slobodan Tekic, Dobrivoje Culibrk, all the persons up and including 150. Is that the group that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say 144?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a different person under this number. It's Todorovic and then Bozic, Mesanovic [phoen]. However on the screen, yes, that's what you are talking about. Miroslav Pijunovic, Slobodan Tekic, Dobrivoje Culibrk, Stojan Zuric [phoen], and others, yes, and they are the persons that we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the following page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the date, date of imprisonment. The fourth from the top, it says, "Transferred on the 17th of July from the Banja Luka prison."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And released on the 6th of August by the Teslic high court, that's what it says here. Take a look at the next column.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I see here. I really don't know how long they spent in prison after they had been transferred from Banja Luka to the Doboj prison, but I know that later on they were released, and now I saw the decision issued by the court with the agreement of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then when there was mention of this case at the meeting in Banja Luka, a conclusion was for the judiciary to continue doing their job. The only thing that you were interested in was not to have your name mentioned in that context and to have it cleared?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there were some rumours and stories that it was I who had sent those men there and that I asked for them to be set free which was not correct. If anyone wishes to claim otherwise, I would like to challenge them to prove that. I know that there was a letter in which my name was typed, but it was signed by Mr. Savic, and, of course, the judge and the prosecutor were the persons who took charge. From that moment onwards, the only thing we could do was to point to certain things, but everybody knows that once a matter goes into the hands of a court it is up to the court to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that in addition to this letter signed by Savic, there was also a letter from the operations group sent to the court in Teslic seeking their release?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the document seeking the release of these persons and I also heard that there were certain threats made, but I personally did not witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at document P1364, tab 9. And this is going to be the last document that I am going to show you. Is this the document that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously this is the document in which there is a request for these men to be released to join armed combat, and should any criminal proceedings be conducted, that that should be done at a later stage. Yes, that's the letter I heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, my last question for you is: Mr. Zupljanin had nothing to do with the release of these persons nor with any subsequent proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had nothing to do with the release, and I also don't believe that he could have had any influence on the subsequent proceedings because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic, I have no questions for you. Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't actually know, one way or the other, do you, Mr. Bjelosevic, whether Mr. Zupljanin had anything do with the release of these men?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he had anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just to make it clear, you don't know whether he did have anything to do with it or didn't have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he had anything to do with it based on all the information that I had about this situation. That's my conclusion and I also -- I never saw any document to support that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In all the investigations that you did into this matter, which I'm going to return to later on, did you ever ask Mr. Zupljanin directly whether he had anything to do with the release of these people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked at this meeting held on the 9th of September and that is when he said that he did not influence this matter at all and that he had no means of deciding on this issue, which, by virtue of his position, that was impossible. Once people are handed over to the court and the prosecution office with the criminal report, nobody can do anything further with regard to that a even if one wanted to have an interview, for example, if an inspector wanted to interview any such person, they had to seek approval from the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to return to this because I want to deal with things in order. I want to go back, Mr. Bjelosevic, to the documents that you have and that you have provided. First of all, the three volumes of notebook that you provided to us or to VWS, are these official notebooks that you had to keep as a member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not an official document. These are my own notes that I took as a kind of reminder for myself. I just noted things down as bullet points. As you can see, this is not an official document and it doesn't comply with any official format. These are just my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there were notes made of meetings that you attended and, as it were, reminders of things that you had to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, that's correct, because I noted down what I thought was important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. But that's not quite an answer to my question. You noted down meetings you attended, the things that you thought were important. That's what you just said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also, as it were, things to do, what might commonly be called a to-do list?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this served as a kind of reminder to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the first diary that you provided to us starts in -- just let me get this right. Sorry, Your Honour. Starts, I think, in May of 1991; is that correct? Can you just confirm, you've got the original there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finishes in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you start that -- carrying and using that notebook from the moment that you became the chief of the Doboj CSB in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the first entry refers to a meeting held on the 27th of May, so I didn't cover the first days of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you started your duties sometime in May of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct. I think it was in the beginning of May. I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The second notebook, is this correct, begins on the 9th of January, 1992? Sorry, second notebook - I beg your pardon, my fault - begins on the 4th of November, 1991? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that? Don't you have entries for the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't know how it was translated, but I believe the witness said the other month, 30th of other month, not November.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 30th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. 30th of October, 1991, perhaps you better tell us, and runs until when?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look. If I see it correctly, the last entry is on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it stops there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this journal ends here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the third one, please, could you tell us the entries there that they run from when to when?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off the mike when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something written before that, but the first date that appears is the 10th of July, 1992, when I was preparing for a meeting in Belgrade and there's also some notes that refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when does that end, that notebook?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically until the end of December of that year, but actually, there is also one entry dated the 5th of January, 1993. The 5th of January is the last entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Bjelosevic, where are your notes for the three-month period, roughly, between the 8th of April, 1992, and the 10th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep notes in that period. I relied mostly on information bulletins and other information gathered by the service relating to hostile activities of paramilitary formations, and so on and so forth. So in that period, as I said earlier, the centre did not have its proper departments and was unable to function properly during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, the 8th of April is roughly -- it's roughly a week after the formation of the Serbian MUP and you are, during the course of April, as we've seen, sending correspondence both to the old BiH MUP and dealing with the new RS MUP. Let's just deal with April. What made you suddenly depart from your usual practice which you had followed slavishly up until then of making notes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not act in any slavish way because that's not my nature. Whatever I noted down was correct and true. I wish you could understand what the situation in the Doboj region was at the time, and perhaps if you would care to look at the video-clips that I provided and the information bulletins, you might get some insight into that because that was an extraordinary situation. There were extraordinary events taking place that were completely contrary to a normal situation, and during that period I was literally stretched between Doboj, Derventa, and the commands of -- in Doboj and Derventa barracks because as I said the situation became extremely complicated. And now I'm telling you that I relied mostly in my work on the summary reports about the security situation on the ground and the information bulletins, and if you saw them yourselves, you could have seen that once an operative finished typing a daily bulletin, then he would add something by hand that happened in the meantime. When I received a bulletin, it would turn out that even new developments happened in the meantime, so I would add new information by hand. So the things were going on at such a pace and speed that I really spent the least of my time in the office trying to make and take down notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but surely, Mr. Bjelosevic, in a period like this whereas you say so much was happening, it was more important that you should keep notes of what you should be doing, where you should be going, and meetings that you were having?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really ask everybody who are making judgements about certain periods and certain events to at least try to perceive the things within the given time and under the given circumstances. Believe me, after 19 years, even I who had gone through this, in hindsight this might seem a little bit different. But at the time that was an a incredible dynamics of developments, the events were stressful, so to put it simply, we could not work and operate in a normal atmosphere. I really don't know -- I don't know what the point is of your question, but if you think that I took some notes and I'm not willing to show them, then I think you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You have, in fact, reached the obvious conclusion that I'm going to put you to. But just before I do, do you agree, Mr. Bjelosevic, that it was in May and June in particular that the serious crimes took place in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you, but let me just remind you that the centre was incapable of functioning properly, and I, myself, as the chief of the centre, was excluded by the Crisis Staff from all these affairs. You will remember the decision of the Crisis Staff which stipulates that all people involved in security business should be placed under the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB, and the only authorised person to organise and run these things in Doboj area was that person. On the other hand, I told you before and I said so to the Honourable Chamber, that I was engaged in military issues and that I wasn't sitting in my office at the centre. I only went there occasionally especially to collect these reports and information, but I wasn't spending all my time in my office nor did I keep any documents on my own because I didn't have anyone to manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have another intervention in the transcript. It says -- it's page 21, line 7. I believe the -- it is recorded: "... jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB, and the only authorised person to organise and run these things in Doboj area was that person." I believe the witness said something different and it is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't make sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can you repeat, please, what you told the Court slowly so that we get correct interpretation, what you were saying about Crisis Staffs order about persons involved in security?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if a lot of criminal offences were being committed at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't repeat the whole answer, please. It's taking long enough as it is. Just repeat what you said about the Crisis Staff decision in respect of security person.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that pursuant to a decision taken by the Crisis Staff it was stipulated that all personnel, or more precisely as it's stated there, individuals and groups involved in security business should be placed under the jurisdiction of the Doboj public security station chief who was the only authorised person for organising and managing security operations and issues in the area of Doboj. Therefore, it means that I was excluded from these affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During this period, the period you say you could do nothing, in fact, you have an alibi for anything that when on for Doboj and during that period, did you rely on the daily bulletins that you have spoken about for the information that you got?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 30th of April, there were no daily bulletins that were kept. I would like to note that the operations duty service of the CSB Doboj which was otherwise part of the milicija department was not functioning at that period of time at all until the CSB was established once again, and that was sometime in July, the end of July. And I think that the operations duty service started operating only from the end of August or the beginning of September within the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, I'll go back to my original question, Mr. Bjelosevic: Wasn't it even more important than it had been before that you kept notes of what you were doing, who you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't important for me. When the operation corridor was underway, and I already told you that I was in a command position, that's the kind of documentation that was kept then, and once the task was completed and this is handed over to the command in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, okay, let's deal with the period that you were in the military, as you -- or working in the military. You don't have any notes at all about any meetings you held with General Talic or anybody else, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I have nothing. Perhaps it would be a good thing for me to recall on this occasion that during exercises before the war we were issued with official notebooks when we attended these exercises, and you will see in my military booklet that I have those exercises recorded. Once the exercise was over, then we had to return these military notebooks before we went back home. Those were the rules in the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry, you are saying, are you, that you had a separate notebook during this period when you were, as you assert, working with General Talic, which you don't have at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not use the word "rokovnik," let that be quite clear. I said that during this command duty there was a certain documentation that was kept, and it was in the form of a work map and there were code documents for keeping communications running. That was after my mission was accomplished. After I finished that duty, then this was handed over to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, I am afraid, what the word means that you mentioned in the Serbian language. But do I understand this, you didn't have a notebook in the way that you have got these notebooks here whilst you were with the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you have any documentation that shows that you were working with the military during the period from the beginning of May until the end of June?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to make a distinction as follows: Between the army, on the one hand, and defence on the other, to make things clearer. In the beginning of May, we started preparing for what would happen later, that is to say Operation Corridor. All information that was relevant to security as far as the strength of the enemy was concerned, was handled by the security service of the military. And separate from that, I used documents from the state security service and then we compared the two, we cross-referenced this information, we made our assessments in order to be able to make the best decision possible for the problem of the corridor. So that was for the army, if I can put it that a way. And then the later period was within the army itself, when I was given a certain direction and certain forces and all the way up until the completion of that task. You will look at the dates, and you will see on the basis of those dates --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry to stop you, but I've just had a notice come up on my LiveNote saying "server connection disabled." I don't know whether that's on anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's the break now anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it's convenient at this point to take the break and see if this technical problem can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, while the witness is on his way in, could you reserve two minutes for me at the end of today, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I interrupted you in your answer because of the problems with LiveNote. The question I asked you was a very simple, straightforward one, namely: Do you have any documentation that shows that you were working with the military during the period from the beginning of May until the end of June, and you were giving a very long answer which I stopped. You had begun to say, and this is at line 17 of page 24: "The later period was within the army itself when I was given a certain direction and certain forces and all the way up until the completion of that task. You will look at the dates and you will see on the basis of those dates," and I interrupted you there. I will let you finish this answer, but can I just say this: I am asking fairly simple, straightforward questions. It would help enormously if you would answer those questions directly, because the longer your answers, the longer you are going to be sitting here.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to be concise. When I spoke about the dates, I said that you can find it out also in this information, and I also wanted to say that I spent a period of time working on the exchange of information and planning of the Operation Corridor. Another period of time I spent on a command duty taking part in the operations, and after that, after that assignment had been completed, I again spent most of my time at the command post in Duga Neva [phoen]. That's where we exchanged and evaluated information about what is about to face our forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, and it can, I suggest to you, be answered yes or no. Do you have any documentation that shows that you were working with the military during the period from the beginning of May until the end of June?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have these documents with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I my return to the question of your notes, but can I just ask you this, Mr. Bjelosevic, you told the Court before you left that you had gone to Zenica because you heard that you are being investigated and that you -- it was at that stage that you started to take copies of documents from the Doboj archives. Did you at the same time get rid of any notes you had for the period April until the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. What should I get rid of?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any notes that might show your involvement, knowledge of, or discussions about the crimes that were being committed in the Doboj area in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Anything that I knew in May and June resulted in reaction from me and you could see that through several orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I just want you to confirm what you told the Court. Your account is that during May and June you were away with the military returning only occasionally to Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that the CSB Doboj was not operating?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move to the other documents, please, however. You kindly provided a breakdown of where you acquired the documents that were part of the Defence exhibits and that you had handed over to the Defence. And I think if we may, we better have, first of all -- yes, well I think the best thing is if we put up the translation and the original of the document. I think it's in Sanction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not an exhibit. I mean, it's not something I'm asking be made an exhibit, but I think it may help if you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, is this right, Mr. Bjelosevic, what we can see ourselves and we've got a translation is that that was the original list that was provided by the Stanisic Defence to us of documents they had acquired from you, and you wrote by the side of it where you had acquired these documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the things that I brought here? Because I can't see anything on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could somebody ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, is it, that's your writing we can see on the list of documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wrote when I left this place. However, either there was some repetition of numbers or I misread something because some front pages have more than one number. That's the reason that I didn't finish the marking of all the documents because I found that some numbers on the document started repeating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I accept that it wasn't always easy to see because there were a number of different numbers on the documents that are in the binder for the Defence which is which, but you say copied from the archive, I think, yes, if we look at item number 1. Are we talking about the Doboj archive?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And those documents that you had copied for you when you -- at the time that you went up to - I want to say Derventa but it's not - Zenica in about 2004 or 2003? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say copied from the archive, were those copies made at the time that you went up to Zenica to see why you were being investigated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I copied a number of documents at that time. I requested them to be copied. Another number of documents I had already had with me because I had them in possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that none of these documents any longer exist in the archives at Doboj. They appear to have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And destroyed at some stage after you had taken these copies. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I really know nothing about that. I never deal with archives and now I hear this for the first time from you. However, let me just say one thing. As far as I know, I don't know exactly when, but your people, your investigators also visited those archives much, much earlier, and I think that I heard that they took some of the documents for your needs. I'm not quite sure whether they made copies or whether they actually removed documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to give evidence, you are absolutely right, as you know because I presume you were there, the Doboj archives have been visited on a number of occasions. Now, next there are documents which you obviously provided but you don't specify where they came from, it's blank. Just see if we look, for example, at item number 13 on this page you've written "copy?"

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is unless I see the document. I think that I probably couldn't remember. I will have to look at the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where we see a complete blank, for example number 15?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's nothing there. I mean, does that mean when you looked at the document you were unable to remember where you had acquired it from?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Or maybe I found another repetition of the number. It's one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, some of the documents, for example, number 25 on the list you say kept copy from 1992 and that entry appears on a number of documents. What was it about these particular documents that made you keep them in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what document that is. I would have to take another look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Quite difficult to sort out myself where they appear in the Defence bundle. Can you give us a general policy, why did you keep some documents in 1992, or copies of some documents in 1992 itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I began to explain. So I don't know exactly about this document but there were some documents, for instance, dispatches or some informations which were then followed by certain activities, meetings, analysis, et cetera. And then a copy of such a document I would keep for my own needs while those activities were being carried out, activities related to certain event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's massive generalisation, Mr. Bjelosevic. Can we have a specific example of what you are talking about? Well, let's have a look. I'm told that the document you wanted to look at is tab 131 in the Defence bundle. 65 ter 231D1.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 131, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we switch from Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a bad copy, but as far as I can see it is about the regulating of the situation related to the reserve police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So exactly, I want to know why that was a document that you kept a copy of in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you straightaway. Maybe you recall that we looked at one document here. It was a document related to the inspection of the public security station in Doboj where it had been found that five reserve policemen, if I'm not mistaken, did not satisfy the conditions stipulated by law, such as having served the national service, and that they hadn't been convicted and similar things. On several occasions various stations were reminded to run those checks and some of them simply didn't want to do that. And I have to tell you that at the time I couldn't assume that this topic would be discussed before this Trial Chamber at some point in future, but trust me, from the very beginning, and it was maybe a bit unusual that a subordinate would reply to orders coming from the minister and trying to draw his attention to some irregularities, but still I was of the opinion at the time that a day would come when all things would have to be explained, especially things related to the fact that the law was not observed. And I simply wanted to have the situation in which such activities could be properly discussed at some future point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Bjelosevic, I accept that entirely. You were, weren't you, during the course of this period, concerned that in the future there might well be trials over what had happened in Doboj in 1992? That's what you said, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about unlawful conduct at various levels. I mentioned and order from the minister, maybe you remember, we mentioned it in my previous testimony, and I wasn't talking only about Doboj. You can take a look at Brod as well. If you want to see what Anto Prkacin explained on the independent television in Banja Luka, you will be able to see that literally confirmed what I said here. Things related to the arrival of his forces from Slavonski Brod, the take-over of the public security station in Bosanski Brod, the disarming of 50-odd policemen, and so and on so forth. I'm talking here about a wider context, not about a particular instance. There were many irregularities in conduct at various places in various levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Can I make it clear to you, Mr. Bjelosevic, as I think you understood, you want to tell this Court about the crimes that were committed about Serbs, and that's the CDs you brought with you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. That as well of course, of course, but it wasn't only that. We are talking about everything that happened, all the crimes that were committed, about all of this unlawful behaviour, about this overall chaotic situation, lack of order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your sentence. If you can pull the microphones down a bit so that they get it and I'll turn mine off.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking only about a narrow area or a particular event. I am talking about everything unlawful that was happening, about crimes that were being committed. I am talking about a totally chaotic situation that prevailed at the time. I've been saying time and again that all of you who are dealing with these matters should try to understand the entirety of the situation and the problems that prevailed at the time. Believe me, that is what I wish. It never crossed my mind, not even at a subconscious level that one should remain silent about any crime or that one crime would justify another. However, you have to understand what kind of times we were living in. Wasn't it criminal to attack a public security station and to disarm the personnel there. And then to have, as you will see in these statements of people who were there, obviously there was this person who was in a position of authority who allowed them to do so. I am sorry, but may I just note one more thing. When I spoke about that during my previous testimony, I apologise for having noticed that, but I did see that you smiled and this made you smile, but believe me, I was chief of a public security station there at the time and that kind of thing happened. There would be formations coming from elsewhere, from an independently recognised state by then and they simply took over your public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can I say straightaway so that you don't have to go on repeating this, I accept that crimes were committed against Serbs, but we are dealing in this trial with your actions. So you issued -- you kept this order, didn't you, because you knew full well that the MUP in Doboj and elsewhere from the meetings you attended was filled with people who were committing criminal offences and who in the past had a criminal record? You knew that at the time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that Ms. Korner repeats her question because she made two suggestions to the witness. One, the people committing crimes, and the people having a criminal record. So the witness should be asked the direct question and then he can answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I accept that, I'll split that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You knew, Mr. Bjelosevic, don't you, that in the ranks of the MUP in the Doboj, the wide of Doboj municipality, there were members of the police who were committing criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had knowledge to that effect. However, you did see what my reactions to that were, that there were oral orders and orders in writing. When we established contact, then the minister also asked for this to be clarified, eliminated, et cetera. Let me try to explain something else to make it clear here. I hope that you do not think that the chiefs of centres selected reserve policemen and that they could individually know about every one of these persons. That was the problem. The local forces, namely the Crisis Staffs and political persons imposed themselves, as you saw in Samac and elsewhere, and they started running the service at one point in time and that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that you want to blame everyone but yourself, Mr. Bjelosevic, but can we stick to the points that I'm asking you about. Did you also know that some of these police officers working in the wider Doboj area who had committed -- who were committing criminal offences had in the past committed criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, this is would really have to be broken down. Policemen who were policemen before the war could not be policemen if they had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything went haywire with the reserve police, starting with that order from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the effect that units of the Territorial Defence and volunteers should be included in the stations. That's when the non-selective manning of reserve police stations started running against the rules that were in force in terms of getting appropriate clearance for the persons who would be involved there. So the code no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it by that you are referring to Pusina's order back in April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were two such orders that pertained to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll -- I'm coming to that later, but can I just ask for the third time the simple question to which I would like a simple answer. However they had come to be in the police, there were people who were authorised officials in the RS MUP in 1992 who had criminal records, were there not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such persons as well in the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether they were in the reserve police or not, they had become, had they not, authorised officials?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already pointed out that we have to make a distinction between the active-duty personnel and the reserve personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll leave this because we could spend even longer. This order of which you kept a copy in 1992 was intended to be part of your defence if you were ever asked about what you had done to show that you issued an order that those who do not meet the specified criteria should be effectively sent to the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I looked at it. I did not perceive from the assumption that somebody would be putting questions to me as to what I had done. Rather, I thought that the questions would be put to those persons why they did not act in accordance with orders and rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Mr. Bjelosevic, that these sorts of orders of which we see numerous examples from you, from Mr. Stanisic and from others are no more than window dressing, that you never expected nor intended that these orders should be carried out?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. I do not agree with one per cent of what you are stating so categorically. You can call the chiefs of stations from the relevant period and the komandirs as well, and you can ask them what I said to them during meetings in addition to what I wrote here. And by now, sorry, but I am talking this as an insult that I was thinking one thing, writing up another thing and doing yet a third thing. I could not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please -- can we go back to the list that you prepared which is in Sanction. Number 84. We maybe better see what the document is. You've written, "Kept one copy for myself in 1992 unlawfully." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have to see what this is all about first. I assume that it has do with an order that is unlawful or a report that was saying that something unlawful had been done. I don't know. I don't know which document that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 36 in your binder. The exhibit number is 1D00257.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. That is one of the orders that is truly unlawful. If you allow me, I would like to give my comment as to why it is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this dispatch, it is actually one of those signed by Mr. Jasarevic and another one, as you had rightly said, was signed by Pusina. Please, how can someone expect you to have a proper structure of the police or milicija, whatever, at the relevant time it was called milicija, when it says here volunteers or persons who are military conscripts that are placed in other ways under the command of, et cetera, et cetera. So what I keep saying, see, the period here is the 8th of April, 1992. That's when it was sent. Mr. Pusina also sent his order at that time. It wasn't that a service was being established, an army was being established to attain military objectives, something similar was happening in Croatia, too. That's the problem. And believe me, that stay of Mr. Hebib's in Brod and that surrender, that was the creation of an army and then since there were such personnel there, you can imagine what kind of people you can run across. And just one more example in this regard. Soon after that, I got a report from the Derventa public security station where precisely these forces that have showed up there as a territorials, as volunteers, entered the public security station, disarmed the people there, the policemen there and threw them out, these policemen, these legal policemen were simply thrown out of the building, they took the building, they looted it, that was it. There was a wave of things like that that were happening. So wasn't it logical for me to keep a dispatch of this kind that was totally unlawful. Again I'm telling you I had no idea that The Hague Tribunal would be established and that we would be discussing this here. However, I was hoping that a proper state would be established where we would clarify such matters. I didn't want to be part of this story. You saw that on the basis of my dispatches that I sent to the then minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the "unlawfully" doesn't mean that you unlawfully had a copy of it. The "unlawfully," and can I check that is the proper translation of the word you used, refers to your -- the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. What I meant was "nazakonito [phoen] naredjenje," unlawful order. That's why I kept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just -- sorry, can we go back to the actual document on Sanction for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just please read out what you actually wrote, word for word, next to document number 84?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
